headline: Consumers pay BDT 300-440 more for 12kg LPG cylinders than official price
summary: Despite the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) setting the price at BDT 2,060, retailers in Dhaka are selling 12kg LPG cylinders for up to BDT 2,500. This widespread overcharging affects millions of households.
details: Consumers in Bangladesh are forced to pay BDT 300 to BDT 440 more than the government-fixed price for a 12kg LPG cylinder. This widespread overcharging is occurring despite the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) increasing commissions for all stakeholders.

The BERC set the price of a 12kg LPG cylinder at BDT 2,060 on November 2. However, a survey of 15 LPG shops in various Dhaka areas found cylinders being sold for BDT 2,350 to BDT 2,500. Forty-five kg cylinders are also being sold for BDT 1,200 to BDT 1,400 above the fixed rate.

When the new prices were set, importers' commission for storage and bottling increased by BDT 82, distributors' by BDT 35 (from BDT 50 to BDT 85), and retailers' by BDT 25 (from BDT 45 to BDT 70). Distributors and retailers claim these commissions are insufficient to cover their costs.

Two top importers state they have increased LPG supply and that action should be taken against those charging extra. Conversely, distributors allege supply shortages and claim some companies are also charging higher prices.

BERC Chairman Jalal Ahmed acknowledged the complaints of overpricing and stated that the commission is investigating. They are also verifying the increase in industrial LPG use and identifying unauthorized sellers who purchase from others to sell at higher prices.

Over 10 million customers in Bangladesh use LPG, with 80% for household cooking. Demand for LPG has surged since 2015 due to the halt in new household gas connections, now exceeding 1.8 million tons annually. The private sector dominates, importing and supplying 99% of the market.

According to LOAB and BERC sources, LPG imports were 158,000 metric tons in August, 156,000 tons in September, and less than 142,000 tons in October. However, an additional 40,200 tons arrived by November 4. LOAB has repeatedly warned distributors against selling at inflated prices.

Some importers cite a global LPG shortage, with supplies from the Middle East almost halted and minimal availability from African countries. Most LPG is now imported from the US at higher costs, including increased shipping fees. They also mention limited storage infrastructure and the risk of losses if global prices drop.

The LPG Traders Cooperative Association argues that the BERC's commission increase for distributors and retailers is inadequate compared to importers. They also claim supply has not increased, leading to long waits at company plants and higher transport costs, making it impossible to sell at fixed prices in Dhaka.

The Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection is aware of the overpricing. Director General Md. Zahirul Islam stated that they are receiving complaints, conducting raids, and imposing fines on sellers.

headline_marked: [[Bangladesh's debt exceeds $204 billion]], now over 40% of GDP, raising fiscal concerns
headline: Bangladesh's debt exceeds $204 billion, now over 40% of GDP, raising fiscal concerns
summary: Debt servicing is projected to become the largest expenditure in the national budget by FY2028-29, potentially pushing Bangladesh into a 'debt trap' similar to Pakistan's situation.
details: Bangladesh's internal and external debt has recently surpassed $204 billion, exceeding 40% of its GDP. This significant increase is largely attributed to the previous government's policies over 15 years, with current administrations also struggling to curb borrowing, particularly domestic debt.

Allocations for principal and interest payments on government debt in the current 2026-27 fiscal year budget are nearly on par with the education and technology sector. Projections indicate that by the 2028-29 fiscal year, debt servicing will become the single largest expenditure category.

This escalating situation risks pushing Bangladesh into a 'debt trap,' where the government must borrow more each year simply to repay existing principal and interest, mirroring the challenges faced by countries like Pakistan.

As of November 2026, Bangladesh's foreign debt stood at $116 billion, over 23% of its total GDP. While this is below the World Bank and IMF's warning threshold of 40% of GDP, other factors suggest a looming danger.

Historically, Bangladesh's foreign debt was less than 15% of GDP until FY2019-20, primarily from soft loans with low interest rates and long repayment periods. Major lenders included the World Bank (38%), ADB (24.5%), and JICA (17%).

Bangladesh has never defaulted on foreign loan installments in 55 years, and until FY2020-21, debt servicing accounted for only 5-6% of the budget. However, a rapid increase in both domestic and foreign borrowing for 'mega projects' in the last decade of the previous administration dramatically accelerated debt accumulation.

While projects like the Padma Bridge, Metro Rail, and Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant are visible achievements, critics argue they conceal stories of immense capital plunder. This alleged corruption during the 'economic development' era has led to an unprecedented rise in debt.

Upon the fall of the previous government in 2024, the total internal and external debt stood at over BDT 18.35 trillion, a staggering increase from BDT 2.76 trillion in 2009. This represents a difference of over BDT 15.58 trillion, accumulated while reporting high per capita GDP growth.

The budget allocation for foreign debt principal and interest payments was around $2.5 billion in FY2023-24, but it has surged to over $4.5 billion in the FY2026-27 budget. This figure is projected to rise further to nearly $6 billion in upcoming fiscal years.

Continued domestic borrowing could push the government's budget deficit beyond 5% of GDP in future fiscal years. A core issue is Bangladesh's revenue-to-GDP ratio, which has plummeted to around 7%, the lowest in South Asia, down from nearly 10% just a few years ago.
